concepts.def: Exchanges energy and matter with surroundings; coasts gain sediment, lose energy.

walkthroughs.body_html: Wave energy varies with fetch: Atlantic waves on western UK coasts have fetch of 5000+ km producing high-energy environments. Sediment inputs include rivers (UK rivers deliver ~10 million tonnes/yr), cliff erosion (Holderness ~1.8 m/yr retreat) and offshore sources.

DRARP framework: Destructive waves erode; Refraction concentrates energy on headlands; Attrition reduces clast size; Rotation moves sediment seasonally; Plunging breakers undermine cliffs. Longshore drift transports along coast at zigzag angle.

Sediment outputs include offshore loss to deep water, aeolian transport inland and human extraction. When inputs equal outputs, the coast is in dynamic equilibrium. Disruption (e.g. dam building reducing river load) triggers adjustment.

mcqs.q: Why do some rivers form deltas and others form estuaries?
options: Deltas form where rivers deposit sediment faster than the sea can remove it (calm seas, heavy load); estuaries form where tidal energy removes sediment (strong tides).
Deltas form on big rivers and estuaries on small ones.
The three cells are tropical, temperate and arctic, named after climate zones.
Deltas form in cold climates and estuaries in warm climates.

mcqs.q: What does Frank's dependency theory argue?
options: Deltas form in cold climates and estuaries in warm climates.
That LICs (periphery) are kept poor by exploitative trade relationships with HICs (core) — underdevelopment is actively produced by capitalism, not a stage that countries grow out of.
Dependency theory says LICs are poor because they depend too much on foreign aid.
Dependency theory is the same as Rostow's modernisation theory.
